title: Epilogue. The Science Behind the Letters

blocks.text: This book is a novel, a sequel to *The Daughter of Two Worlds*. Aya, Andrés, Lía, the clone, Nexum, the correspondence bridge and the worlds visited here are fiction. What follows is not. Here we separate, as carefully as we can, what already existed in 2026 (with date and source) from what still belongs to the realm of speculation or dream. Nothing written in these pages replaces the judgement of a healthcare professional.

blocks.text: **There are planets around other stars, and they are genuinely studied, not only in novels.** On 23 November 1995, *Nature* published “A Jupiter-mass companion to a solar-type star” by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz (https://www.nature.com/articles/378355a0). It was the first convincing detection of a planet orbiting a Sun-like star: 51 Pegasi b. That work changed astronomy and, in 2019, earned them the Nobel Prize in Physics.

blocks.text: On 24 August 2016, *Nature* published “A terrestrial planet candidate in a temperate orbit around Proxima Centauri”, led by Guillem Anglada-Escudé (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature19106). Proxima Centauri is the nearest star to the Sun. The planet, Proxima b, has a minimum mass of about 1.3 times that of Earth and completes an orbit in about 11.2 days, in a zone where, in principle, liquid water could exist. That does not mean there is a sea there, or a fisherman, or a letter. It means that the Sun's closest neighbour has at least one rocky world at an interesting distance, and that its star, an active red dwarf, can lash it with flares.

blocks.text: On 22 February 2017, NASA announced, and on 23 February *Nature* published, the work of Michaël Gillon and his team, “Seven temperate terrestrial planets around the nearby ultracool dwarf star TRAPPIST-1” (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature21360). Seven Earth-sized planets around a small star, some forty light years away. Several of them could, given the starlight they receive, harbour liquid water if they had the right atmosphere. On 27 March 2023, *Nature* published “Thermal emission from the Earth-sized exoplanet TRAPPIST-1 b using JWST” (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-05951-7). The James Webb Space Telescope measured the heat of TRAPPIST-1 b's dayside and found a temperature of about 500 kelvin, more consistent with little or no atmosphere than with an envelope of air spreading the heat around. Seeing a planet is a fact. Imagining its cities is not.

blocks.text: **In clinical trials, a person can move a cursor or a robotic arm with the activity of their brain.** On 16 May 2012, *Nature* published “Reach and grasp by people with tetraplegia using a neurally controlled robotic arm” by Leigh R. Hochberg and colleagues, using the investigational BrainGate system (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature11076). Two people with tetraplegia controlled a robotic arm in three dimensions; one of them managed to bring a bottle of coffee to her mouth. On 9 January 2023, *JAMA Neurology* published the SWITCH study, “Assessment of Safety of a Fully Implanted Endovascular Brain-Computer Interface for Severe Paralysis in 4 Patients”, on the Stentrode, an interface placed through a blood vessel, without opening the skull, in four patients with severe paralysis in Australia (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2799839). In May 2023, the FDA cleared Neuralink to begin its first clinical trial in humans, and in January 2024 the first implant of its interface was carried out, according to the company's own update of 12 April 2024 (https://neuralink.com/updates/prime-study-progress-update/). On 8 May 2024, Neuralink identified the first participant, Noland Arbaugh, who was using the device to move a cursor and operate a computer (https://neuralink.com/updates/prime-study-progress-update-user-experience/). That is a brain–computer interface: signals from the brain translated into commands for a machine. It is not receiving another person's life into one's mind.

blocks.text: **There is serious research on memory, including prostheses that assist it, and it is not the same as a letter from the stars.** On 22 March 2012, *Nature* published “Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall” by Xu Liu, Steve Ramirez, Susumu Tonegawa and the rest of the team (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature11028). In mice, reactivating a specific group of hippocampal neurons with light was enough to evoke the memory of a fear. On 15 June 2011, the *Journal of Neural Engineering* published “A cortical neural prosthesis for restoring and enhancing memory” by Theodore W. Berger, Robert E. Hampson, Sam A. Deadwyler and colleagues (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3141091/): in rats, a prosthesis that copied hippocampal firing patterns was able to restore or improve performance on a memory task when that region was blocked. On 28 March 2018, the same journal published “Developing a hippocampal neural prosthetic to facilitate human memory encoding and recall” by Robert E. Hampson and his team from Wake Forest and the University of Southern California (https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1741-2552/aaaed7). In epilepsy patients who already had electrodes implanted for clinical reasons, stimulation with the pattern of a correct encoding improved performance on episodic memory tests by around 35–37 per cent. It is a remarkable step. It is also a reinforcement of that person's own memory in a specific task, not the transfer of someone else's life, nor an artificial brain that holds all of a man's memories.

blocks.text: **A mammal has been cloned from an adult cell; people are not cloned.** Dolly the sheep was born on 5 July 1996. On 27 February 1997, *Nature* published the work of Ian Wilmut and colleagues, “Viable offspring derived from fetal and adult mammalian cells” (https://www.nature.com/articles/385810a0). In Spain, Law 14/2006 of 26 May on assisted human reproduction techniques expressly prohibits “the cloning of human beings for reproductive purposes” (Article 1.3) (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2006-9292). (The quotation from the Spanish law is our own translation.) A young clone of Andrés, with an artificial brain and all his memories, is a premise of this novel, not an existing or authorised procedure.

blocks.text: **Nobody has sent a human being to another star system.** The Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 probes, launched in 1977, have reached the threshold of interstellar space; they are not crewed craft, and they took decades to leave, only just, the Sun's domain. In 2026 there is no crewed journey to Proxima b, to TRAPPIST-1 or to any of the worlds this novel imagines. The singing oceans, the twilight planet, the forest that remembers, the chorus without I and those who never end are invention. Some of their landscapes are inspired by real scientific ideas (for example, that a planet very close to its star could have one side in permanent day and another in permanent night), but the peoples, the cities and the letters that come from there are not, today, in any catalogue.

blocks.text: **There is no bridge that deposits one person's experience in another's mind.** The interfaces of 2026 read, with difficulty and in clinical settings, intentions to move or, in very specific trials, help to encode one's own memory. They do not copy a consciousness. They do not install an artificial brain loaded with an entire life story. They do not allow anyone to “live something without living it” the way Andrés receives the letters. Eternal life, as the epilogue of the first book already said, is not an approved therapy.

blocks.text: This novel imagines that, decades after 2060, some of these impossibilities are debated or crossed, because the laws and techniques of one age do not always coincide with those of the next. That is a premise of fiction, not a prediction.

blocks.text: Andrés receives worlds he has never set foot on. The clone walks worlds that the man on the shore only drinks. Lía asks who did the walking, and doesn't close the harbour. Aya doesn't receive the letter and still holds up the house. That question (what it is to live something without living it, what is left of a self when its memory is shared, who the father is if both remember the same storm) is ethical, not technical, and no scientific paper will settle it. The science of 2026 can already point to planets light years away, give a person with paralysis back control of a cursor and, in a trial, strengthen a memory. It cannot yet tell us what we should do with a home and with the whole universe, if one day we were offered both.
